paragraphs: Since the particular will acts constantly against the general will, the government continually exerts itself against sovereignty. The greater this exertion becomes, the more the constitution changes; and since in this case there is no other corporate will to create an equilibrium by resisting the will of the prince, sooner or later the prince must inevitably suppress the Sovereign and break the social compact. This is the unavoidable, inherent defect which, from the very birth of the body politic, tends ceaselessly to destroy it, just as old age and death end by destroying the human body.
There are two general ways in which government degenerates: _i.e._ when it contracts, or when the State is dissolved.

Government contracts when it passes from the many to the few, that is, from democracy to aristocracy, and from aristocracy to royalty. This is its natural tendency.[1] If it took the backward course from the few to the many, it could be said to relax; but this reverse sequence is impossible.

In fact, a government changes its form only when its energy has run out and left it too weak to keep what it has. If a government widened its reach and relaxed its grip at the same time, its force would fall to nothing, and it would last even less. So the spring must be wound up and the hold tightened as it gives way; otherwise the State it supports will come to grief.
The dissolution of the State can come about in either of two ways.

First, when the prince ceases to administer the State in accordance with the laws and usurps the sovereign power. A remarkable change then occurs: it is not the government but the State that contracts. I mean that the great State is dissolved and another is formed within it, composed solely of the members of the government, which becomes, for the rest of the people, merely master and tyrant. So the moment the government usurps sovereignty, the social compact is broken, and all private citizens recover by right their natural liberty and are forced, but not bound, to obey.

The same thing happens when the members of the government each usurp separately the power they should exercise only as a body. That is just as great a breach of the laws, and it produces even worse disorders. There are then, so to speak, as many princes as there are magistrates, and the State, no less divided than the government, either perishes or changes its form.

Once the State is dissolved, the abuse of government, whatever form it takes, goes by the common name of _anarchy_. To be more precise: democracy degenerates into _ochlocracy_, aristocracy into _oligarchy_, and I would add that royalty degenerates into _tyranny_. This last word, however, is ambiguous and needs explaining.

In everyday speech, a tyrant is a king who governs with violence and with no regard for justice and law. In the exact sense, a tyrant is a private individual who takes royal authority for himself without any right to it. The Greeks understood the word this way: they used “tyrant” without distinction for good and bad princes alike, whenever their authority was not legitimate.[2] _Tyrant_ and _usurper_ are thus perfectly synonymous terms.

To give different things different names, I call the man who usurps royal authority a _tyrant_ and the man who usurps sovereign power a _despot_. The tyrant is he who thrusts himself in against the laws in order to govern according to the laws; the despot is he who sets himself above the laws themselves. Thus the tyrant cannot be a despot, but the despot is always a tyrant.

It is most astonishing that the Venetians, after more than twelve hundred years of existence, still seem to be at the second stage, which they reached with the _Serrar di Consiglio_ in 1198. As for the ancient Dukes who are brought up against them, it is proved, whatever the _Squittinio della libertà veneta_ may say of them, that they were in no sense Sovereigns.

A case certain to be cited against my view is that of the Roman Republic, which, it will be said, followed exactly the opposite course, passing from monarchy to aristocracy and from aristocracy to democracy. I do not take this view of it at all.

What Romulus first set up was a mixed government, which soon degenerated into despotism. For particular reasons the State died before its time, as newborn children sometimes perish without reaching manhood. The expulsion of the Tarquins was the true birth of the Republic. But at first it took on no lasting form, because by not abolishing the patriciate it left half its work undone. In this way hereditary aristocracy, the worst of all legitimate forms of administration, remained in conflict with democracy, and the form of the government, as Machiavelli has shown, was fixed only when the tribunate was established. Only then was there a true government and a genuine democracy. In fact, the people were then not only Sovereign but also magistrate and judge; the senate was only a subordinate tribunal, to temper and concentrate the government; and the consuls themselves, though they were patricians, first magistrates and absolute generals in war, were in Rome itself no more than presidents of the people.

From that point the government followed its natural tendency and leaned strongly toward aristocracy. The patriciate, we may say, abolished itself, and the aristocracy was found no longer in the body of patricians, as at Venice and Genoa, but in the body of the senate, which was made up of patricians and plebeians, and even in the body of tribunes once they began to usurp an active function. For names do not change facts, and when the people has rulers who govern for it, whatever name they bear, the government is an aristocracy.

The abuse of aristocracy led to the civil wars and the triumvirate. Sulla, Julius Caesar and Augustus became in fact real monarchs; and finally, under the despotism of Tiberius, the State was dissolved. Roman history thus confirms the principle I have laid down, rather than refuting it.

[For all those are called and considered tyrants who hold perpetual power in a State that has known liberty.] Aristotle, it is true, (_Nicomachean Ethics_, Book viii, chapter x) distinguishes the tyrant from the king by the fact that the former governs in his own interest and the latter only for the good of his subjects. But not only did all Greek authors in general use the word _tyrant_ in a different sense, as appears most clearly in Xenophon’s _Hiero_; it would also follow from Aristotle’s distinction that, from the beginning of the world until now, there has not yet been a single king.
